nameStory: The barnacle-eating dorid gets its name from its favorite food - barnacles! This little sea slug has specialized feeding habits, using its rasping tongue to scrape away at barnacle shells and feast on the soft animals inside. It's also called the rough-mantled doris because of the bumpy texture covering its back, which looks like a textured cloak or mantle.
description: The barnacle-eating dorid is a small, soft-bodied sea slug that lives in New England's rocky coastal waters. These shell-less marine snails typically measure about half an inch to an inch long and have an oval, flattened body. Their backs are covered in small bumps and tubercles that give them a rough, warty appearance, usually in shades of white, cream, or pale yellow. Like other nudibranchs (pronounced NEW-dih-branks, meaning 'naked gills'), they breathe through feathery gill structures on their backs.

idTips.label: Bumpy back texture
idTips.description: The upper surface feels rough and bumpy to the touch, covered in small tubercles and projections that look like tiny warts

idTips.label: Feathery gills
idTips.description: Look for delicate, feather-like gill structures arranged in a circle on the back end - these retract quickly when disturbed

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Body is typically cream, white, or pale yellow with a translucent quality that lets you sometimes see internal structures

idTips.label: Oval body shape
idTips.description: Has a flattened, oval form that's wider in the middle and tapered at both ends, like a small slug

idTips.label: Two sensory tentacles
idTips.description: A pair of club-shaped tentacles at the front end that feel around for food and detect chemicals in the water

habitat: Look for barnacle-eating dorids in New England's rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters, especially where barnacles are abundant. They're commonly found clinging to rocks, pilings, and jetties from the low tide line down to about 30 feet deep. You'll often spot them in tide pools or on barnacle-encrusted surfaces in harbors and rocky shores from Maine to Connecticut.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found feeding on barnacles in tide pools during low spring tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot during low tides, often visible on rocks and pilings feeding during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper water as temperatures drop, though still findable in protected tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper waters or well-protected areas, rarely seen in typical tide pooling spots during this season.

funFact: This tiny sea slug can completely dissolve a barnacle's limestone shell using acid it produces in its stomach, then sucks out the soft barnacle like a marine smoothie - essentially turning one of the ocean's toughest-shelled creatures into liquid lunch!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, pale nudibranchs, but the combination of bumpy texture and circular gill arrangement is distinctive. Remember: 'Bumpy back, barnacle snack' - the rough texture is your best clue, unlike smooth-bodied sea slugs.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Latin, referring to how these sea slugs wear their breathing organs on the outside of their bodies like external lungs. Don't confuse these marine dorids with terrestrial slugs - they're completely different groups that just happen to have similar soft, elongated body shapes.
compareHints: The barnacle-eating dorid differs from its close relative, the fuzzy Onchidoris, primarily in texture and feeding habits. While both have bumpy backs, the fuzzy Onchidoris has more hair-like projections and typically feeds on bryozoans rather than barnacles. The barnacle-eating dorid's tubercles are more rounded and wart-like, while the fuzzy species has more elongated, spiky projections that give it a fuzzier appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Fuzzy Onchidoris is much more textured than its relative the barnacle-eating dorid, which has a smoother body surface.
